What happens when nobody replies?

The program asks Alice at 09:00. Choose what she does. 
// A decision with a declared default. Why Norn?

Every ending is handled

Whoever you ask is autonomous. They may answer, refuse, run out of time, try and fail, or lose the authority to act. A request ends in exactly one of six replies, and the type checker rejects a program that skips one or lets a request drop.

Waiting is cheap

A program can wait for a person, a merged pull request or next Tuesday. Waiting suspends it, for weeks if need be, across restarts and deploys. Nothing polls, and a deadline belongs to the request, not to whoever happens to be watching.

Programs, not graphs

You write ordinary functional code with a ReScript-flavoured surface: immutable bindings, variants, pattern matching and inferred types. Reminders, schedules, approvals and follow-ups are library functions written in Norn itself.

The six ways a request can end

ReplyWho actedWhat it means
Answered(x)the participantThey answered, and x is the answer.
Refused(why)the participantThey explicitly declined.
NoReplythe clockThe request's own deadline passed with no answer.
Broke(why)the participantThey tried, and could not do it.
Cancelledthe programThe program called the request off.
Revokedthe authorityThe authority behind the request was lost.

Write it in Norn

Teams keep rebuilding the same few mechanisms: reminders, schedules, approval cards, “waiting for your reply”, “keep going until it's done”. Underneath they are one relationship. Someone asks, someone answers or doesn't, and the work goes on.

Agents settle it between themselves

One agent drafts, another looks for what does not hold, and they go round until the reviewer says Sound. A person is one kind of participant, never a required step.

Open in the playground 
// Two agents settle a design between themselves. The reviewer is asked for// exactly Sound, or Flawed with the reason: a run reports the type the// program uses its report as.type verdict = Sound | Flawed(string)let rec settle = draft =>  switch run(@codex, "Find what does not hold in this design", ~about=draft)->wait? {  | Sound => Answered(draft)  | Flawed(why) => settle(run(@claude, "Revise the design", ~about=draft, ~context=why)->wait?)  }settle(run(@claude, "Draft the design for request identity")->wait?)

Follow up, then hand over

Ask an agent. If an hour passes, the wait ends but the request stays open, so the same question moves to a person instead of being asked twice.

Open in the playground 
// A follow-up that hands the same request over from an agent to a person.// Handing over moves who continues; it does not undo what the agent may// already have done, which the host still reconciles.let q = ask(@codex, "Is the build machine still overheating?")let reply = switch q->waitUntil(1h) {| Some(r) => r| None => q->handOver(@alice)->wait}say(doc"ops#machines", reply?)

Wait on facts in the world

A pull request merges, a release picks it up, a machine updates. The program waits on each fact in turn, then gives the next step to an agent, or to a person when the chain stalls.

Open in the playground 
// A chain of facts in the world, then an agent.let pr = merged("acme/api#1436")->waitswitch released(Beta, ~containing=pr)->waitUntil(1d) {| Some(release) =>  machineUpdated(~machine="win-builder", ~atLeast=release.version)->wait  run(@codex, "Check out acme/api on win-builder and confirm the long-path fix")->wait| None => run(@alice, "#1436 did not reach a beta within a day: find out why")->wait}

Keep a standing duty

Every day, and whenever CI fails on main. One failed run reaches the author and the duty carries on.

Open in the playground 
// A standing duty.every(1d)->or(ciFailed("acme/api"))->forEach(_ => run(@auto, "Check production health and fix the riskiest issue")->wait)

Keep going until it is done

An agent saying “done” and the work being done are checked separately. The loop wakes on the next activity or after two hours, whichever comes first.

Open in the playground 
// Keep going until a judged condition holds.let rec push = () => {  let report = run(@claude, "Move #1439 forward until it is merged and verified live")->wait?  if judge("merged and verified live", ~about=report)->wait? {    Answered(report)  } else {    prActivity("acme/api#1439")->or(after(2h))->wait    push()  }}push()?

Coordination, not orchestration

No conductor

Each program belongs to a person, an agent or a document, and waits on others the way a team member does. The dependency graph is whatever the runtime can draw from where programs are waiting.

One level above agent frameworks

Participants are people and complete agents of any kind, not model calls or tools. How an agent thinks is the agent's business. Norn describes how they get the work done together.

Capabilities, not restrictions

Norn is Turing complete, and a program touches the world only through a handful of effects. Spending, mailing and deploying happen inside agent runs, under their own permissions.

Hosts carry it

A host says who the participants are, how requests reach them, which events exist and where the ledger of requests is kept. xMatrix is the first host. The language does not depend on it.

The name

In Norse myth, the Norns sit beneath the world tree Yggdrasil and spin the threads of fate for gods and people alike, settling what comes next and when. Norn was also a real language: the Norse tongue of Orkney and Shetland, last spoken in the 18th century. A language in which people and agents weave their work together borrows its name.
